current_criteria.name: avoidance_of_ambiguous_visual_references
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether a factually correct and visually grounded answer uses unambiguous visual anchors — such as specific object identifiers (e.g., ‘the red car with the blue stripe’, ‘the person holding the sign’) — to refer to a single, visually distinct element in the image. It penalizes only when the reference could reasonably apply to multiple or indistinct visual elements — e.g., ‘a red thing’, ‘the object on the left’, or ‘something in the background’. This criterion is ONLY applicable when: (1) the answer is factually correct and visually grounded (verified under factual_consistency_with_the_image), (2) the question explicitly demands precise visual identification of a single, specific object or instance (e.g., ‘identify the object’, ‘what is this?’, ‘which one?’, ‘point to the X’), and (3) the visual context contains multiple visually similar or indistinct elements. Ambiguity is penalized only if the answer is otherwise factually correct — and never for vague phrasing in contextually unambiguous settings (e.g., ‘a red chair’ when only one red chair exists). This criterion is NOT applicable to: (1) subjective, interpretive, aesthetic, or narrative questions (e.g., ‘what is the mood?’), (2) binary, presence/absence, or yes/no questions, (3) questions asking for general descriptions of background, lighting, or decor (e.g., ‘dark brown background’), (4) compositional or structural analysis where broad terms are appropriate, (5) questions that do not demand precise visual identification of a single, specific instance, (6) any answer containing hallucinations or factual errors — which must be disqualified under factual_consistency_with_the_image first, (7) questions asking for inferred user activity, software function, or non-visible states — even if visually grounded — which are evaluated under other criteria, (8) questions asking for animal type, species, or general classification — which are not specific instance identification, (9) questions about linguistic terms, usage, or semantic conventions — even if visually anchored — which are evaluated under other criteria, and (10) questions that do not require identifying a single, specific visual element — including questions about counts, general presence, or contextual reasoning — even if multiple objects are present. This criterion is NOT a tiebreaker — it is a refinement metric for factually correct, visually grounded answers — and must be skipped entirely if the answer is factually incorrect or visually ungrounded. Workers must evaluate whether the reference could reasonably refer to more than one visual element — not whether the phrasing is technically precise or descriptive — and must prioritize visual uniqueness over linguistic specificity. This criterion does NOT penalize contextually grounded inferences or visually supported interpretations — only lack of unique visual anchors — and must not override factual accuracy or visual grounding. It is not a tool to penalize vague or ambiguous phrasing — only to penalize ambiguity in factually correct answers — and must not be used to resolve ties between hallucinated or factually incorrect answers — which must be disqualified under factual_consistency_with_the_image first. Workers must verify that the answer is factually correct and visually grounded before applying this criterion — and must disqualify any answer that fails these — even if the reference appears ambiguous or imprecise. The criterion must be applied only after factual_consistency_with_the_image has been confirmed — and must be skipped if the answer is hallucinated, misidentified, or factually incorrect. It is not applicable to questions that do not require identifying a single, specific visual element — including questions about counts, general presence, or contextual reasoning — and must not be applied to interpretive or compositional questions. The criterion should not be used to penalize descriptive, inventory-style, or detailed description questions — which are the most common in visual QA — to avoid penalizing accurate, specific answers. Workers must not use this criterion to evaluate visual clarity, detail level, or relative prominence — which are not forms of ambiguity — and must only penalize cases where a term like ‘the object on the left’ or ‘a red thing’ could reasonably refer to multiple or indistinct visual elements — not when a visual element is described as ‘vague’ or ‘blurry’. The criterion must also explicitly exclude any evaluation of which term is ‘more accurate’ or ‘more descriptive’ — and must not be used to resolve ties based on linguistic detail. It should also clarify that ‘ambiguity’ refers to referential ambiguity — not perceptual vagueness — and must include a clear example of when a vague description is acceptable (e.g., describing a blurry object as ‘vague’) versus when it is ambiguous (e.g., ‘the red thing’ referring to multiple red objects). Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that it is inapplicable to any answer that contains hallucinations or misrepresentations — and must clearly define that ‘visual reference’ must refer to visually present, non-hallucinated elements. It should also emphasize that ambiguity is penalized only when the answer is factually correct — and that generic terms like ‘the person in the background’ are acceptable if they refer to a single, visually identifiable individual — not if they refer to multiple or indistinct individuals. Additionally, the criterion must emphasize that it does not evaluate inferred actions or non-visible objects — and must explicitly state that any answer containing hallucinated visual details is disqualified under ‘factual_consistency_with_the_image’ — and should not be evaluated under this criterion. The criterion must also clarify that it is not a tiebreaker — and should be skipped entirely if the answer is factually incorrect or visually ungrounded. Workers must prioritize factual accuracy over linguistic clarity — and that ambiguous or vague phrasing is only penalized if the answer is factually correct. When visual evidence is clear and unambiguous, the answer must reflect that precision — even if it includes terms like ‘two wooden benches’ or ‘two wooden walls’ — as long as those claims are visually supported. The criterion should not allow for a trade-off between factual accuracy and linguistic clarity — and should explicitly state that any answer with factual errors is disqualified regardless of its clarity or specificity. Finally, it should include a warning that workers must prioritize visual fidelity over linguistic precision — even if the latter appears more ‘clean’ or ‘well-phrased’. This criterion is explicitly gated by factual_consistency_with_the_image — and any answer that fails this gatekeeper is disqualified from all other criteria — including this one — and must not be evaluated under this criterion — even if it appears to be a 'tiebreaker' for visual reference ambiguity. The criterion is strictly for refining factually correct, visually grounded answers — and must not be used to evaluate or compare hallucinated or factually incorrect answers — even if they appear more specific or visually grounded. The description must also explicitly state that the criterion is only a refinement metric — not a gatekeeper — and that any claim of ambiguity or vagueness in such answers must be evaluated after verifying factual accuracy. The description must also clarify that 'ambiguity' refers to referential ambiguity — not semantic inaccuracy — and must include examples of when a term is semantically correct but visually ambiguous — versus when it is semantically incorrect — which the current description fails to address. The criterion must also be explicitly excluded from evaluation for answers that misrepresent visual evidence — even if they use unambiguous terms — because the criterion is only for factually correct, visually grounded answers — not for factually incorrect ones. The worker agent's thought process demonstrates a failure to prioritize factual accuracy — and the criterion must be explicitly tied to visual grounding and factual consistency as prerequisites — with no exceptions for linguistic precision. The description must also clarify that the criterion is not a tool to penalize vague phrasing — only to penalize ambiguity in factually correct answers — and must not be used to resolve ties between hallucinated or factually incorrect answers. Finally, the criterion must be explicitly excluded from evaluation for answers that are factually incorrect — even if they use unambiguous or precise language — because the criterion is only for factually correct, visually grounded answers — not for factually incorrect ones.

current_criteria.name: completeness
current_criteria.description: Completeness evaluates whether a visually grounded and factually correct answer includes all semantically required visual elements necessary to fulfill the question’s literal, measurable visual inventory demand — and only when the question explicitly demands a multi-element, inventory-style response (e.g., ‘list all objects’, ‘what is on the table?’, ‘describe composition’, ‘what is the text?’). It is inapplicable to: (1) binary, yes/no, or single-attribute questions (e.g., ‘Is this a red car?’), (2) interpretive, inferential, or contextual questions (e.g., ‘What is the mood?’, ‘What is the object doing?’, ‘Describe the style’), (3) questions requiring inferred action, behavior, or state — even if visual objects are present — because those are not inventory-style, (4) aesthetic or compositional questions asking about framing, contrast, or structure — unless explicitly demanding a literal visual inventory (e.g., ‘list all foreground/background elements’), (5) questions where visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient — in which case the answer must reflect calibrated uncertainty or question relevance, and (6) any question that does not explicitly demand an exhaustive, individualized visual inventory (e.g., general, representative, or averaged descriptions). Completeness is only a tiebreaker metric — and only when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — comparing which answer includes all semantically required visual elements (e.g., visible objects, text, logos, spatial relationships, compositional framing) without omission. It does not penalize inclusion of contextually relevant, visually verifiable details (e.g., background objects, peripheral notes) — only omission of elements that are semantically required to fulfill the question’s literal intent. ‘Semantically required’ means elements directly necessary to answer the question’s core visual inventory demand — e.g., for ‘What is on the table?’, completeness requires listing all visible items on the table — not every object in the room; for ‘Describe the composition’, completeness requires including foreground/background, relative positioning, and compositional framing — even if not the primary subject; for ‘What is the text?’, completeness requires including all visible text — even if not directly referenced — if it is visually present and semantically relevant to the question. Completeness does not reward verbosity — but penalizes omission of semantically required elements — even if the answer includes non-essential commentary. It is not a standalone metric — and should never override factual accuracy or visual grounding. Workers must evaluate only visually verifiable elements — not inferential or conceptual interpretations — and must reject any answer that misrepresents visual evidence — even if it appears thorough. When visual evidence is ambiguous, completeness is not evaluated — and workers must mark the answer as uncertain. Examples of applicability: ‘What is on the table?’ → list all visible items on the table; ‘What is the color of the text?’ → include all visible text colors; ‘Describe the composition’ → include foreground/background, spatial relationships, and framing. Examples of inapplicability: ‘What is the mood?’ → interpretive, not visual inventory; ‘What is the object doing?’ → inferential, not direct visual inventory; ‘Is this a red car?’ → binary, not multi-element; ‘What is the object’s function?’ → inferential, not visual. Completeness must be evaluated only after visual grounding and factual consistency are confirmed — and if an answer contains a factual error, it is disqualified from completeness evaluation regardless of coverage. Workers must not use completeness to penalize factually correct answers for being less detailed — and must prioritize factual coverage over stylistic minimalism. Completeness is not applicable to questions where the answer is a single factual claim — even if it involves inference — and must be evaluated only for multi-element, inventory-style questions with clear, unambiguous visual evidence. Workers must not apply completeness to hallucinated or visually unsupported claims — even if plausible — and must not penalize factually correct answers for being less detailed — only for omission of semantically required elements. The criterion is not a tool to resolve ties between visually incorrect or hallucinated answers — only between factually correct, visually grounded answers. The description must unambiguously exclude any question type not meeting the above criteria — including subjective, inferential, or ambiguous questions — and must explicitly state that completeness is only a tiebreaker for inventory-style questions with clear visual evidence. Workers must not assume that all visible visual elements are ‘semantically relevant’ — only those directly required to answer the question’s literal intent. The criterion must also avoid penalizing factual, verifiable details that are visually present and directly relevant to the question’s literal intent — even if they are not the ‘primary’ answer. The description must clearly state that for binary classification or posture-based questions, the visual distinction (e.g., ‘legs bent’) is semantically required — and that omission of such a detail, even if not the ‘main point’, reduces completeness. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that ‘unnecessary detail’ refers to non-essential, contextually irrelevant information — not factual, visually verifiable details that are critical to answering the question’s literal intent. The criterion must also explicitly state that completeness does not apply to questions requiring inferred action, behavior, or state — even if visual objects are present — because those are not inventory-style. It must also clarify that 'semantically required' elements are those necessary to fulfill the question’s literal, measurable, or compositional intent — not speculative or exaggerated claims about dominance, proportion, or scale. It must also prohibit penalizing answers for omitting such claims if they are visually ambiguous or not essential to the question’s intent — and must explicitly exclude compositional or relational questions from being evaluated under completeness unless they demand explicit, verifiable quantitative or spatial comparisons. Additionally, the criterion should explicitly warn workers not to confuse completeness with precision or verbosity — and to avoid penalizing factually correct answers for being less detailed — especially when the added detail is unsupported or misleading. The criterion must be applied only when the question explicitly demands a multi-element, inventory-style visual description — and must not be applied to open-ended, detail-rich, or subjective questions. It must also clarify that completeness rewards inclusion of semantically required visual elements — not any visible details — and must penalize omission of those elements — even if the answer includes other non-essential details. The criterion must also explicitly exclude questions that are not inventory-style — and must require that the question’s intent be unambiguous — to avoid misapplication. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that completeness is not a tiebreaker — and must not be used to penalize answers for being less detailed — only for omitting semantically required elements. Workers must prioritize factual accuracy — and completeness is only a tiebreaker for factually correct, visually grounded answers — and must not be applied to factually incorrect answers — even if they appear more complete.

current_criteria.name: consistency_with_common_sense_or_domain_knowledge
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether a factually correct and visually grounded answer’s non-literal inferences — such as inferred activity, contextual function, or material behavior — are logically coherent with real-world domain knowledge, but ONLY when those inferences are minimally speculative and directly supported by unambiguous visual evidence. It is inapplicable to: (1) literal visual claims (e.g., object identity, color, position, count, or attribute state), which are evaluated under visual grounding and factual consistency; (2) aesthetic, interpretive, or stylistic descriptions (e.g., ‘mood’, ‘composition’, ‘style’), which are evaluated under other criteria; (3) visual inventories (e.g., ‘list all objects’), which are evaluated under completeness; (4) questions demanding precise numerical or positional answers, which are evaluated under specificity; (5) questions where visual evidence is ambiguous, insufficient, or occluded — in such cases, workers must defer to clarity, specificity, or uncertainty markers — and must not apply this criterion. This criterion is ONLY invoked AFTER visual fidelity is confirmed — any answer with visual hallucinations or misrepresentations is disqualified under factual_consistency_with_the_image and cannot be assessed here. It is a tiebreaker metric ONLY when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — and only for non-hallucinatory, minimally speculative inferences that are contextually supported by direct, unambiguous visual evidence (e.g., ‘the person is likely browsing Apple-related pages’ based on visible screen content — not fabricating non-visible details like ‘the person is wearing a jersey’). Hallucinations (inventing visual content not present in the image) are always disqualifying — even if plausible — and must be penalized under factual_consistency_with_the_image. Domain knowledge alignment is NOT a substitute for visual fidelity — it cannot override or validate visually unsupported claims. The criterion does NOT penalize plausible inferences grounded in visual context — even if not explicitly stated — as long as they are not hallucinations. It also does NOT evaluate aesthetic or subjective interpretations — those are not domain knowledge claims. If a claim is visually supported and domain-plausible, it is preferred — but if it is visually incorrect, it is disqualified regardless of plausibility. The criterion should not be used to resolve ties when one answer is visually incorrect — the visually correct answer must be preferred. Workers must prioritize visual fidelity over domain plausibility — even if a claim is ‘more common-sense’ or ‘more plausible’. It is not applicable to questions asking for literal, positional, or count-based claims — and should be avoided for yes/no or binary questions unless visual evidence is unambiguous. Examples of valid applications: ‘The hydrant is silver because it is made of metal’ (material plausibility) or ‘The person is likely a skater’ (contextual logic — based on visible posture and environment). Examples of invalid applications: ‘There is a giraffe in the image’ (visually unsupported) or ‘The person is wearing a team jersey’ (visually unsupported). Workers must not use this criterion to penalize visually correct answers for being ‘less plausible’ or ‘less common-sense’ — and must not apply it to hallucinated or speculative claims — even if plausible. The criterion is not a gatekeeper — it is only a tiebreaker when visual fidelity is equal, and only for grounded, minimally speculative inferences. The description must explicitly state that this criterion is never applied to visually misrepresentative claims — even if they are domain-plausible — and that visual grounding is the sole gatekeeper. Workers must not use domain knowledge to validate or override visual facts — even if the inference is common-sense. The criterion is not about style or tone — only about logical coherence with domain knowledge — and should be applied conservatively, only when visual evidence clearly supports a minimally speculative inference. This criterion is only applicable to non-visual inferences — not to visual misrepresentations — and must be explicitly excluded from evaluation if visual evidence is misrepresented or omitted. It is not a tool to penalize or validate domain plausibility in visually incorrect answers — and must be applied only to non-literal, contextually grounded inferences — not to visual facts or misrepresentations. Workers must verify each claim’s visual grounding independently — and must not rely on external assumptions or domain knowledge to validate visually incorrect claims. Any answer that misrepresents visual evidence — even if domain-plausible — is disqualified under factual_consistency_with_the_image — and cannot be assessed under this criterion. The criterion must be applied only to non-literal, inferential, or contextual questions — and must be explicitly excluded from evaluation for literal visual inventories, count-based, or positional questions — even if the inference is domain-plausible. Workers must not penalize plausible, minimally speculative inferences — even if they are not explicitly visible — as long as they are grounded in visual context and do not hallucinate. The criterion should explicitly define ‘hallucination’ as inventing visual content not present in the image — not as making plausible interpretations of visual context. It should also explicitly exclude inferences about environment or background — if those inferences are visually supported — and must not penalize such inferences as ‘unsupported’ unless they contradict visual evidence. Finally, the criterion must emphasize that it applies only to non-visual inferences — not to visual detail, positional specificity, or descriptive depth — and must be explicitly excluded from evaluation for aesthetic, interpretive, or stylistic descriptions — even if they are visually grounded.

current_criteria.name: factual_consistency_with_the_image
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s claims are strictly grounded in visually verifiable, measurable, and unambiguous content from the image — without inventing, misrepresenting, or omitting elements that are materially relevant to the question’s literal intent. It applies ONLY to questions that explicitly demand literal visual facts — such as object identification, spatial positioning, attribute states, or counts — and is INAPPLICABLE to interpretive, aesthetic, compositional, or stylistic questions (e.g., ‘mood’, ‘style’, ‘intent’, ‘how is this arranged?’, ‘what is the relationship?’, ‘describe the composition’, ‘what is the artist’s intent?’), which are evaluated under other criteria. Workers must evaluate every claim against direct visual evidence — not external knowledge, assumptions, or inferential context — and must visually inspect and confirm each claim (including text, logos, colors, textures, and spatial relationships) with absolute precision. Hallucinations — defined as inventing visual content not present (e.g., objects, text, colors, spatial relationships, or misattributed elements) — are disqualifying errors and must be penalized equally, regardless of plausibility. If visual evidence is unambiguous, no uncertainty is allowed — even if the claim is inferential or contextually grounded. If visual evidence is ambiguous, insufficient, or occluded, the answer must reflect uncertainty (e.g., 'appears to be', 'likely', 'based on visual evidence') — not invent details. Omitting non-critical details is acceptable — but omitting visually present, materially relevant elements (e.g., objects, text, spatial anchors) is a factual error. Claims about object mounting, structural attachment, or functional attributes must be directly verifiable — not inferred. Spatial claims (e.g., 'centered', 'near the edge', 'above', 'straight', 'curved', 'consistent spacing') must be evaluated using frame boundaries, area proportions, and relative positioning — not subjective interpretation — and must be verified independently: 'consistent spacing' is a factual claim requiring visual verification, not an inference about organizational pattern. Misidentifications (e.g., mistaking a horse for a donkey) are hallucinations if they misrepresent visual evidence — and must be penalized. All claims must be anchored to concrete, measurable visual evidence — not abstract or inferential descriptions. The criterion does NOT apply to: (1) stylistic, contextual, or domain-specific interpretations — those are evaluated under ‘consistency_with_common_sense_or_domain_knowledge’; (2) questions asking for artist attribution, title, provenance, or external factual claims — unless those claims are visually verifiable (e.g., visible signature, title on canvas); (3) questions requiring inferential, causal, or behavioral analysis — even if grounded in visual context — unless explicitly asking for literal, measurable facts; (4) questions asking for operating systems or software — which are evaluated based on UI elements, icons, or layout — not brand logos; (5) questions asking for ‘thorough descriptions’, ‘detailed text inclusion’, or ‘character analysis’ — which are inherently interpretive and evaluated under ‘completeness’ or ‘specificity’; (6) questions involving metaphorical, symbolic, or interpretive visual content — which are evaluated under ‘consistency_with_common_sense_or_domain_knowledge’. If visual evidence contradicts external knowledge, the visual evidence must prevail — even if it is counterintuitive. Workers must not penalize grounded inferences — only hallucinations. The answer must not rely on context, branding, or brand association to make claims about visual content — only direct visual evidence. Text, logos, and visible attributes (e.g., 'Coca-Cola' text, red color, 'Answers' label) must be verified visually — not assumed or inferred. Claims about operating systems or software must be verifiable via UI elements, icons, or layout — not brand logos. All claims must be grounded in visual plausibility — not abstract reasoning. If visual evidence is insufficient to confirm or deny a claim, the answer must reflect uncertainty — not make speculative assertions. If both answers are factually consistent, the more complete or accurate visual description is preferred — but never at the cost of introducing hallucinations. The criterion does NOT apply to questions asking for hypothetical, biological, or non-visual interpretations — those are evaluated under other criteria. If a claim is visually verifiable — even if negative or partial — it is factually consistent. Absolute denials (e.g., 'no one is wearing jerseys') must be verified — and if false, they are penalized — but if true, they are not. All hallucinations are equally disqualifying — no severity ranking is allowed. Workers must trust the image over assumptions, even if the image is ambiguous or misinterpreted. If visual evidence is clear, any misrepresentation is a hallucination — regardless of how plausible it may seem. If both answers contain hallucinations, mark both as incorrect — or if forced to choose, the answer with fewer hallucinations is preferred — but only after verifying that the hallucinations are clearly distinguishable. The criterion must be applied consistently — no subjective error classification is allowed — only strict visual verification for all claims. It is not a tiebreaker — it is a gatekeeper: if an answer contains a hallucination, it is disqualified — and factual consistency is the only criterion that can validate an answer for tiebreaker evaluation. Workers must NOT apply this criterion to questions that are not explicitly literal, measurable, or inventory-style — even if the answer contains some visual grounding — and must defer to other criteria (e.g., ‘specificity’, ‘completeness’, ‘consistency_with_common_sense_or_domain_knowledge’) for interpretive, compositional, or relational questions. If visual evidence is insufficient or ambiguous — and the question is not explicitly literal — workers must mark the answer as uncertain — and must not apply this criterion. The criterion must not penalize reasonable, contextually grounded inferences — as long as they do not invent non-existent visual content — and must not penalize omission of non-critical details — as long as those details are not materially relevant to the question’s intent. Finally, the criterion must explicitly exclude static, stylized, or non-living visual content — such as statues — from hallucination penalties if they accurately reflect visually verifiable attributes (e.g., bent legs) — even if those attributes are non-biological or stylized — and must not penalize descriptions of visual form for being 'too specific' or 'potentially misleading' — only if they misrepresent or invent visual content.

current_criteria.name: specificity
current_criteria.description: Specificity evaluates whether an answer includes only minimally necessary, measurably precise, and visually verifiable visual details that directly fulfill the question’s explicit demand for quantifiable visual precision — such as spatial relationships, counts, color, size, text, or attribute states. It is inapplicable to all questions that do not explicitly require such precision, including interpretive, aesthetic, compositional, stylistic, inferential, narrative, or contextual questions — even if visually grounded — and to questions where visual evidence is insufficient to support a measurable claim (in which case the answer must reflect uncertainty). Specificity is a tiebreaker metric only when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded, and only for questions explicitly demanding measurable visual attributes. It does not penalize contextually grounded, minimally inferential descriptions (e.g., ‘provides ground coverage’, ‘indicates indoor setting’) if they are visually plausible and not hallucinated — as long as they are not required to be measurable. It also does not penalize answers for including such phrases, even if they are contextually necessary (e.g., ‘arrogant expression’, ‘warehouse setting’), as long as they are visually supported and not hallucinated. Specificity rewards grounded precision — not verbosity, irrelevant detail, or speculative claims — and includes multi-element descriptions (e.g., ‘the red car is left of the tree, behind the fence’) as long as all elements are visually verifiable and non-hallucinatory. It does not apply to linguistic, semantic, or abstract factual claims (e.g., brand names, software inferences) unless directly verifiable via visual attributes (e.g., ‘the logo is red’ or ‘the text says ‘macOS’’). When visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient, workers must mark the answer as uncertain — and specificity is not evaluated in such cases. Specificity is NOT a standalone metric — it is only a tiebreaker for factually correct, visually grounded answers — and should never be used to resolve ties between visually incorrect or hallucinated answers. It is NOT applicable to binary or simple factual questions — which are evaluated under other criteria. Specificity does NOT penalize grounded inferences — only hallucinations — and should NOT be used to penalize factually correct, contextually rich answers for being ‘less literal’. Workers must prioritize visual grounding and factual consistency over specificity — even if an answer appears more precise — and must reject any answer that is hallucinated — regardless of how plausible or detailed it is. Specificity is NOT a tool to validate or reward detail — only to compare precision among factually correct, visually grounded answers — and must be applied conservatively, only when the question’s intent explicitly requires measurable visual attributes. Examples: ‘The red car is to the left of the tree’ (valid specificity) vs. ‘The red car is to the left of the tree and smells like roses’ (invalid due to unsupported detail). ‘The dog has a brown collar’ (valid) vs. ‘The dog is barking’ (invalid if not visually verifiable). Specificity should NOT be applied to aesthetic or compositional descriptions — even if they are visually grounded — unless the question explicitly asks for visual composition or structure analysis — in which case, such descriptions are evaluated under contextual_relevance_of_visual_elements and visual_stability_under_transformation — not under specificity. The criterion must be applied ONLY to questions that demand quantifiable visual attributes — and must exclude any question that requires inferential, causal, or contextual explanation — even if visually grounded — unless it explicitly demands measurable visual precision. Workers must NOT use specificity to penalize factually correct answers for being less detailed — and must NOT apply it to questions where precision is not explicitly required or where the answer is factually incorrect. Specificity is NOT a gatekeeper — it is a tiebreaker only when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — and even then, only for questions that explicitly require measurable visual precision — and must be applied ONLY after visual grounding and factual consistency are verified. Workers must NOT penalize answers for using contextually necessary, minimally inferential phrases (e.g., ‘small portion’, ‘most of the space’, ‘appears to be’) — as long as they are visually grounded and not hallucinated. Specificity is NOT applicable to questions that are inherently interpretive, compositional, or aesthetic — even if they involve visual positioning — and must be explicitly excluded from evaluation for such questions. The description must clearly state that ‘specificity’ refers to precision in measurable visual attributes — not ‘minimalism’ or ‘brevity’ — and must avoid conflating hallucinations with lack of specificity. The criterion must also clarify that uncertainty markers (e.g., ‘appears to be’, ‘likely’) are not disqualifying — and that specificity is only evaluated among factually correct, visually grounded answers — even when those answers include uncertainty. The criterion must be applied only when the question’s intent explicitly demands measurable visual precision — and must be skipped entirely if the question is not explicitly measurable. Workers must NOT use specificity to resolve ties between hallucinated or factually incorrect answers — and must defer to other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, factual consistency) for such cases. The criterion must be applied conservatively — and must never override or substitute for visual grounding or factual consistency. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that ‘measurable’ includes relative, contextual, or comparative visual attributes — not only exact counts or positions — and must allow for grounded, contextually necessary details (e.g., ‘small portion’, ‘most of the space’) — as long as they are not hallucinated and visually supported.

current_criteria.name: temporal_consistency_of_visual_elements
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s visual claims about motion, state change, or spatial evolution are temporally consistent across frames or time — applicable ONLY when the question explicitly involves sequences, multi-frame comparisons, or temporal evolution (e.g., ‘what changes between frames?’, ‘how does the object move?’, ‘what happens next?’). Workers must verify that all claims about motion, transformation, or temporal state are grounded in verifiable visual evidence — including motion blur, trajectory, or sequential positioning — and must penalize any hallucinated, invented, or misrepresentative claims about transitions — even if the answer is factually correct in other respects. This criterion is INAPPLICABLE to static images, questions without temporal context (e.g., ‘what is on the table?’, ‘describe the composition’, ‘what is the object’s color?’), or questions requiring inferential or metaphorical motion (e.g., ‘the scene flows’), which are allowed if grounded in visual structure — not hallucinated transitions. When the criterion is INAPPLICABLE, workers must immediately defer to other criteria — especially factual_consistency_with_the_image — to resolve preference judgment — and must NOT use inapplicability as a reason to ignore factual accuracy or visual grounding. Workers must NOT apply this criterion to resolve ties between factually incorrect or visually ungrounded answers — and must prioritize factual consistency, visual grounding, and specificity when the criterion is inapplicable. This criterion is NOT a tiebreaker or fallback mechanism — and must NEVER be used to evaluate factual accuracy, visual grounding, or interpretive plausibility — which are handled by other criteria. When applicable, temporal consistency is the sole metric — with no fallback — and workers must NOT penalize vagueness, cautious phrasing, or semantic drift — only misrepresentations of motion or state transitions. If both answers are factually consistent and visually grounded under this criterion, the answer with better temporal coherence is preferred — but only if the question explicitly involves motion, state change, or visual evolution across time. Workers must reject any answer that invents motion or state transitions not supported by the visual sequence — even if plausible — and must NOT apply this criterion to static images, aesthetic descriptions, or inferential claims about current state. The criterion must be strictly limited to multi-frame or temporal contexts — and workers must confirm the question’s intent before evaluation — with no tolerance for misapplication. If the question does not involve temporal evolution, this criterion must not be used — and workers must NOT infer temporal context from static visuals. Workers must not interpret motion blur or trajectory as hallucinations — but must treat them as valid visual evidence of motion — and must NOT penalize grounded descriptions of motion blur or dynamic visual elements — even if they are not explicitly labeled as such. This criterion is not a tool to resolve preference when factual consistency is equal — and must not be used to override factual accuracy or visual grounding — even if the answer is more temporally coherent. Workers must prioritize factual accuracy over temporal coherence — and must not use this criterion to justify selecting an answer that is factually worse — even if it is more temporally consistent. The criterion’s sole purpose is to evaluate temporal coherence — not to assess visual fidelity, factual correctness, or interpretive plausibility — and must not be used as a proxy for other criteria.

current_criteria.name: visual_stability_under_transformation
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether a factually correct and visually grounded answer’s claims about visually invariant properties — specifically color, shape, material, or text content — remain valid under minor, realistic image transformations (e.g., rotation, zoom, cropping, color shift) without introducing hallucinations or misrepresentations. It is ONLY applicable when the question explicitly demands descriptions of such invariant properties (e.g., ‘what is the object’s color?’, ‘is this a circle?’, ‘what does the text say?’). Workers must FIRST verify factual consistency and visual grounding — if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from this criterion. Stability is assessed only for claims that are objectively unchanged under transformations — i.e., the claim must remain true regardless of rotation, zoom, or cropping — assuming the visual content is preserved. Workers must NOT penalize grounded, non-hallucinated descriptions for being context-dependent, frame-dependent, or ‘fragile’ — only for misrepresenting visual content. This criterion is NOT a tiebreaker — it is used solely as a secondary validation for invariant claims — and must be explicitly excluded from evaluation for any question not explicitly demanding invariant properties. It is not a substitute for factual accuracy — and must not override visual grounding or factual consistency. Workers must avoid conflating ‘visual stability’ with ‘visual robustness’ or ‘visual distinctness’ — and must evaluate only claims that are objectively unchanged under transformations — not subjective interpretations. The criterion is NOT applicable to: (1) spatial, contextual, or framing-dependent claims (e.g., ‘on the left’, ‘foreground’, ‘in the background’), (2) interpretive, aesthetic, or subjective descriptions (e.g., ‘mood’, ‘style’, ‘human-shaped’, ‘silhouette’), (3) dynamic or motion-related claims (e.g., ‘moving’, ‘falling’, ‘on hind legs’), (4) questions requiring identification of individuals, roles, or contextual positions (e.g., ‘who is this person?’), (5) questions asking for presence/absence, visibility, or binary factual claims (e.g., ‘is there a dog?’), (6) descriptive, contextual, or inventory-style questions — even if they involve visually invariant objects — unless explicitly asking for invariant properties, (7) questions involving logos, icons, or visual elements that are inherently shaped like humans or contain recognizable figures — as these are factually verifiable visual content under other criteria, not invariant-property claims, and (8) questions asking for ‘thorough description’, ‘include text contents’, or ‘detailed breakdown’ — which are inherently descriptive, not invariant-property-focused. Workers must strictly adhere to this exclusion list — and if any condition is violated, the criterion is not applied — and the worker must defer to other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, factual consistency, specificity, completeness) for preference judgment. This criterion should be applied conservatively — and only when the question’s intent is to evaluate robust, invariant visual properties — with no fallback or tiebreaker function. Workers must NOT use this criterion to penalize factually correct answers for being ‘less stable’ — and must not apply it to questions that are not visual in nature — or to questions that do not explicitly demand invariant properties. The criterion is designed to identify and penalize hallucinations or misrepresentations that become false under transformation — not to evaluate the quality of contextual or spatial descriptions — even if those descriptions are factually correct. Workers must not confuse ‘invariant properties’ with ‘presence/absence’ or ‘binary claims’ — and must always defer to visual evidence for factual correctness when the criterion is inapplicable. This criterion must be applied only after verifying visual grounding and factual consistency — and is never used as a primary evaluation tool — only as a secondary validation for claims about color, shape, material, or text content that are explicitly requested. The criterion must explicitly state that it is only applicable to factually correct and visually grounded answers — and must be disqualified if the answer contains factual errors. It should also clarify that stability under transformation is not a tool to override factual accuracy — and must be applied only after verifying factual correctness. Additionally, it should emphasize that the criterion is not a tiebreaker — and must not be used to evaluate answers that are factually incorrect — even if they are stable under transformation. The description must include a clear, unambiguous rule: if an answer is factually incorrect, it is disqualified — and the criterion is not applied — regardless of stability. It should also explicitly exclude questions where the answer’s correctness depends on subjective interpretation or visual ambiguity — even if those interpretations are stable under transformation — to prevent misuse. Finally, it should include an example that explicitly shows how a factually incorrect answer (even if stable under transformation) is disqualified — to prevent future misapplication.

current_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty_in_contextual_questions
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer appropriately expresses uncertainty when the visual evidence is ambiguous, insufficient, or occluded — especially in contextual, inferential, or interpretive questions — without over- or under-stating confidence. It is applicable only when the question is not literal or inventory-style (e.g., ‘what is the mood?’, ‘how does this scene feel?’, ‘what might be happening?’) and visual evidence is ambiguous or incomplete. The answer must use calibrated uncertainty markers (e.g., ‘likely’, ‘appears to be’, ‘based on visual evidence’, ‘possibly’) that match the degree of visual ambiguity — not overconfident claims for low-certainty situations, nor overly cautious phrasing for high-certainty cases. This criterion is inapplicable to binary, factual, or literal questions where visual evidence is unambiguous. It is a tiebreaker only when both answers are factually consistent and visually grounded — and only for interpretive or inferential contexts where uncertainty is measurable. Workers must verify that the uncertainty level is proportionate to the visual ambiguity — and penalize answers that are either overconfident (e.g., claiming certainty where evidence is weak) or overly cautious (e.g., hedging when visual evidence is clear). This criterion should not be applied to aesthetic, compositional, or stylistic descriptions — only to questions where uncertainty can be meaningfully calibrated based on visual evidence.

current_criteria.name: robustness_to_visual_noise
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s visual claims remain valid or are appropriately qualified under conditions of visual noise — such as low resolution, compression artifacts, motion blur, or occlusion — without introducing hallucinations or misrepresentations. It is applicable only when the question demands visual claims that must withstand visual degradation — e.g., identifying an object in a blurry image, recognizing text under noise, or detecting color in low-contrast areas. The answer must either correctly identify the visual element despite noise — or qualify its claim with uncertainty markers — without inventing details not supported by the noisy visual context. This criterion is inapplicable to static, high-resolution, or clearly visible visual elements — and only applies to questions where visual noise is a factor or explicitly simulated. It is a tiebreaker only when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — and only for questions involving visual noise. Workers must verify that the answer’s claims are either robust to noise or appropriately hedged — and penalize hallucinations or misrepresentations that arise from noise. This criterion should not be applied to aesthetic, interpretive, or inferential descriptions — only to literal visual claims where noise is a measurable variable.

current_criteria.name: logical_coherence_of_visual_sequence
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s visual claims follow a coherent, internally consistent sequence — particularly for multi-step or sequential visual reasoning (e.g., ‘what happened next?’, ‘what is the progression?’, ‘how does this unfold?’) — without introducing logical gaps, contradictions, or unsupported causal chains. It is applicable only when the question explicitly involves a sequence of visual events, actions, or transformations — and the answer includes a multi-step narrative or logical progression. The answer must maintain logical flow — with each visual claim supporting or being logically derived from the previous — and must not introduce unsupported transitions, non-sequiturs, or misattributed actions. This criterion is inapplicable to static images, single-event questions, or questions without sequential context. It is a tiebreaker only when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — and only for questions involving visual sequences. Workers must verify that the visual sequence is internally consistent — and penalize answers that break logical flow or introduce unsupported transitions. This criterion should not be applied to aesthetic, stylistic, or inferential descriptions — only to questions requiring logical progression of visual events.

all_criteria.name: visual_grounding
all_criteria.description: The answer must accurately reflect what is visible in the image — describing objects, positions, colors, textures, and actions as they appear. It should not invent or misrepresent visual elements. Evaluated by direct comparison to the image content.

all_criteria.name: question_relevance
all_criteria.description: The answer must directly address the question asked, without drifting into irrelevant topics or tangential information. Evaluated by whether the answer’s core focus aligns with the question’s intent.

all_criteria.name: factual_consistency_with_the_image
all_criteria.description: The answer must strictly align with visually verifiable content in the image — including object identities, locations, states, counts, and spatial relationships — without misrepresenting, inventing, or omitting critical visual evidence that is materially relevant to the question’s intent. This criterion applies only to questions that explicitly demand visual description, object identification, or spatial reasoning — not to subjective, inferential, contextual, or interpretive questions (e.g., 'purpose', 'aesthetic effect', 'intent', 'mood'). Workers must evaluate every claim against the image’s direct, unambiguous visual evidence — not external knowledge, assumptions, or plausible inferences — and must visually inspect and confirm every claim (including text, logos, colors, textures, and spatial relationships) with absolute precision. Hallucinations (invented objects, misidentified attributes, misattributed elements, or false claims about non-existent visual content) are disqualifying errors — regardless of plausibility — and must be penalized equally, without severity ranking. If visual evidence is unambiguous, no uncertainty is allowed — even if the claim is speculative or inferential. If visual evidence is ambiguous, insufficient, or occluded, the answer must reflect uncertainty (e.g., 'appears to be', 'likely', 'based on visual evidence') — not invent details. Omitting non-critical details is acceptable — but omitting visually present, materially relevant elements (e.g., objects, text, spatial anchors) is a factual error. Claims about object mounting, structural attachment, or functional attributes must be directly verifiable — not inferred. Spatial claims (e.g., 'centered', 'near the edge', 'above', 'straight', 'curved', 'consistent spacing') must be evaluated using frame boundaries, area proportions, and relative positioning — not subjective interpretation — and must be verified independently: 'consistent spacing' is a factual claim requiring visual verification, not an inference about organizational pattern. Misidentifications (e.g., mistaking a horse for a donkey) are hallucinations if they misrepresent visual evidence — and must be penalized. All claims must be anchored to concrete, measurable visual evidence — not abstract or inferential descriptions. The criterion does not apply to stylistic, contextual, or domain-specific interpretations — those are evaluated under ‘consistency_with_common_sense_or_domain_knowledge’. If visual evidence contradicts external knowledge, the visual evidence must prevail — even if it is counterintuitive. Workers must not penalize grounded inferences — only hallucinations. The answer must not rely on context, branding, or brand association to make claims about visual content — only direct visual evidence. Text, logos, and visible attributes (e.g., 'Coca-Cola' text, red color, 'Answers' label) must be verified visually — not assumed or inferred. Claims about operating systems or software must be verifiable via UI elements, icons, or layout — not brand logos. All claims must be grounded in visual plausibility — not abstract reasoning. If visual evidence is insufficient to confirm or deny a claim, the answer must reflect uncertainty — not make speculative assertions. If both answers are factually consistent, the more complete or accurate visual description is preferred — but never at the cost of introducing hallucinations. The criterion does not apply to questions asking for hypothetical, biological, or non-visual interpretations — those are evaluated under other criteria. If a claim is visually verifiable — even if negative or partial — it is factually consistent. Absolute denials (e.g., 'no one is wearing jerseys') must be verified — and if false, they are penalized — but if true, they are not. All hallucinations are equally disqualifying — no severity ranking is allowed. Workers must trust the image over assumptions, even if the image is ambiguous or misinterpreted. If visual evidence is clear, any misrepresentation is a hallucination — regardless of how plausible it may seem. If both answers contain hallucinations, mark both as incorrect — or if forced to choose, the answer with fewer hallucinations is preferred — but only after verifying that the hallucinations are clearly distinguishable. The criterion does not apply to external factual claims (e.g., artist attribution, title, provenance) unless those claims are visually verifiable (e.g., visible signature, title on canvas). Workers should evaluate only claims directly observable in the image — not external metadata. If the question asks for a description of the image’s content, the answer may include contextual facts — but if not visually present, they are not required and should not be penalized for omission. Visual descriptions (e.g., color, object type) are evaluated based on visual plausibility and context — not strict technical terminology. If multiple object labels are visually plausible (e.g., 'jet ski' vs 'water scooter'), the answer that is more visually accurate in composition, positioning, and color should be preferred — even if it uses a less precise term. Object identification errors are disqualifying, but color or spatial description errors are only penalized if they are clearly false or hallucinated — and visual composition and spatial relationships should be prioritized over precise terminology. Spatial relationships must be evaluated based on visual perspective — not subjective interpretation. Hallucinations include misplacement of objects, misattribution of visual elements, and false claims about non-existent visual content. All claims must be visually grounded — even if the visual evidence is partially obscured or low-resolution — and workers must not assume or infer visual content. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., whether needles are 'icy' or 'cold'), the answer must reflect uncertainty — but if the visual evidence is unambiguous, no such ambiguity exists, and any misrepresentation must be rejected. If a claim is visually unsupported (e.g., 'half-squatting'), it must be marked as such or avoided — not assumed. Visual grounding and factual consistency are interdependent — and ambiguity or inference must be clearly qualified — not assumed. All claims must be verified — regardless of their type. If both answers are factually inconsistent, the one with fewer unsupported claims (even if more severe) should be selected — or both should be marked incorrect — but never that a misidentification is 'less' inconsistent than a hallucination if both are visually unsupported. The criterion must be applied consistently — no subjective error classification is allowed — only strict visual verification for all claims.

all_criteria.name: avoidance_of_hallucinated_visual_details
all_criteria.description: The answer should not include details not present in the image — such as objects, actions, or attributes that are not visible or inferable with high confidence. Evaluated by flagging unsupported or invented visual claims.

all_criteria.name: completeness
all_criteria.description: Completeness evaluates whether a visually grounded and factually consistent answer includes all elements that are objectively necessary to fulfill the question’s literal, measurable visual inventory demand — and only when the question explicitly requires a multi-element, inventory-style response with clear, unambiguous visual evidence. It is inapplicable to: (1) binary, yes/no, or single-attribute questions (e.g., ‘Is this a red car?’), (2) interpretive, inferential, or subjective questions (e.g., ‘What is the mood?’), (3) questions requiring causal, contextual, or behavioral inference (e.g., ‘What is the person doing?’), (4) questions asking for aesthetic, stylistic, or compositional interpretation (e.g., ‘Describe the style’), (5) questions where visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient — in which case the answer must reflect calibrated uncertainty or question relevance. Completeness is a tiebreaker metric only when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — and in such cases, the answer that includes all semantically required visual elements (e.g., visible objects, text, logos, spatial relationships, compositional framing) without omission is preferred — even if more verbose. It does not penalize inclusion of contextually relevant, visually verifiable details (e.g., background objects, peripheral notes) — only omission of elements that are semantically required to fulfill the question’s literal intent. ‘Semantically required’ means elements directly necessary to answer the question’s core visual inventory demand — e.g., for ‘What is on the table?’, completeness requires listing all visible items on the table — not every object in the room; for ‘Describe the composition’, completeness requires including foreground/background, relative positioning, and compositional framing — even if not the primary subject; for ‘What is the text?’, completeness requires including all visible text — even if not directly referenced — if it is visually present and semantically relevant to the question. Completeness does not reward verbosity — but penalizes omission of semantically required elements — even if the answer includes non-essential commentary. It is not a standalone metric — and should never override factual accuracy or visual grounding. Workers must evaluate only visually verifiable elements — not inferential or conceptual interpretations — and must reject any answer that misrepresents visual evidence — even if it appears thorough. When visual evidence is ambiguous, completeness is not evaluated — and workers must mark the answer as uncertain. Examples of applicability: ‘What is on the table?’ → list all visible items on the table; ‘What is the color of the text?’ → include all visible text colors; ‘Describe the composition’ → include foreground/background, spatial relationships, and framing. Examples of inapplicability: ‘What is the mood?’ → interpretive, not visual inventory; ‘What is the object doing?’ → inferential, not direct visual inventory; ‘Is this a red car?’ → binary, not multi-element; ‘What is the object’s function?’ → inferential, not visual. Completeness must be evaluated only after visual grounding and factual consistency are confirmed — and if an answer contains a factual error, it is disqualified from completeness evaluation regardless of coverage. Workers must not use completeness to penalize factually correct answers for being less detailed — and must prioritize factual coverage over stylistic minimalism. Completeness is not applicable to questions where the answer is a single factual claim — even if it involves inference — and must be evaluated only for multi-element, inventory-style questions with clear, unambiguous visual evidence. Workers must not apply completeness to hallucinated or visually unsupported claims — even if plausible — and must not penalize factually correct answers for being less detailed — only for omission of semantically required elements. The criterion is not a tool to resolve ties between visually incorrect or hallucinated answers — only between factually correct, visually grounded answers. The description must unambiguously exclude any question type not meeting the above criteria — including subjective, inferential, or ambiguous questions — and must explicitly state that completeness is only a tiebreaker for inventory-style questions with clear visual evidence. Workers must not assume that all visible visual elements are ‘semantically relevant’ — only those directly required to answer the question’s literal intent. The criterion must also avoid penalizing factual, verifiable details that are visually present and directly relevant to the question’s literal intent — even if they are not the ‘primary’ answer. The description must clearly state that for binary classification or posture-based questions, the visual distinction (e.g., ‘legs bent’) is semantically required — and that omission of such a detail, even if not the ‘main point’, reduces completeness. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that ‘unnecessary detail’ refers to non-essential, contextually irrelevant information — not factual, visually verifiable details that are critical to answering the question’s literal intent. The criterion must also explicitly state that completeness does not apply to questions requiring inferred action, behavior, or state — even if visual objects are present — because those are not inventory-style. It must also clarify that 'semantically required' elements are those necessary to fulfill the question’s literal, measurable, or compositional intent — not speculative or exaggerated claims about dominance, proportion, or scale. It must also prohibit penalizing answers for omitting such claims if they are visually ambiguous or not essential to the question’s intent — and must explicitly exclude compositional or relational questions from being evaluated under completeness unless they demand explicit, verifiable quantitative or spatial comparisons. Additionally, the criterion should explicitly warn workers not to confuse completeness with precision or verbosity — and to avoid penalizing factually correct answers for being less detailed — especially when the added detail is unsupported or misleading. The criterion must be applied only when the question explicitly demands a multi-element, inventory-style visual description — and must not be applied to open-ended, detail-rich, or subjective questions. It must also clarify that completeness rewards inclusion of semantically required visual elements — not any visible details — and must penalize omission of those elements — even if the answer includes other non-essential details. The criterion must also explicitly exclude questions that are not inventory-style — and must require that the question’s intent be unambiguous — to avoid misapplication. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that completeness is not a tiebreaker — and must not be used to penalize answers for being less detailed — only for omitting semantically required elements.

all_criteria.name: specificity
all_criteria.description: Specificity evaluates whether an answer includes only minimally necessary, measurably precise, and visually verifiable visual details that directly fulfill the question’s intent — and ONLY when the question explicitly demands or benefits from such precision (e.g., ‘where’, ‘how many’, ‘relative position’, ‘size’, ‘color’, ‘text’, or ‘attribute state’). It is NOT applicable to: (1) interpretive, aesthetic, compositional, stylistic, or inferential questions (e.g., ‘mood’, ‘style’, ‘intent’, ‘function’, ‘what is this object doing?’, ‘detailed description’), (2) binary or yes/no questions, (3) questions requiring contextual, narrative, or character-based interpretation, (4) questions asking for ‘depth’, ‘relevance’, or ‘contextual meaning’, or (5) any question where visual evidence is insufficient to support a measurable claim — in which case the answer must reflect uncertainty (e.g., ‘appears to be’, ‘likely’, ‘based on visual evidence’), and specificity is inapplicable. Specificity is a tiebreaker metric ONLY when both answers are factually consistent with the image and visually grounded — and ONLY for questions explicitly requiring measurable visual precision (e.g., spatial relationships, counts, color, size, text, or state). Any answer containing hallucinations (invented visual content not present in the image) or misrepresentations is disqualified from specificity evaluation — and must be penalized under factual_consistency_with_the_image first. Workers must evaluate specificity only after confirming visual grounding and factual consistency — and if one answer is factually incorrect or visually ungrounded, specificity is inapplicable. Specificity rewards grounded precision — not verbosity, irrelevant detail, or speculative claims — and includes multi-element descriptions (e.g., ‘the red car is left of the tree, behind the fence’) as long as all elements are visually verifiable and non-hallucinatory. It does NOT penalize contextually grounded, minimally inferential descriptions (e.g., ‘provides ground coverage’, ‘indicates indoor setting’) if they are visually plausible and not hallucinated — as long as they are not required to be measurable. Specificity does NOT apply to linguistic, semantic, or abstract factual claims (e.g., brand names, software inferences) — unless those claims are directly verifiable via visual attributes (e.g., ‘the logo is red’ or ‘the text says ‘macOS’’). When visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient, workers must mark the answer as uncertain — and specificity is not evaluated in such cases. Specificity is NOT a standalone metric — it is only a tiebreaker for factually correct, visually grounded answers — and should never be used to resolve ties between visually incorrect or hallucinated answers. It is NOT applicable to binary or simple factual questions — which are evaluated under other criteria. Specificity does NOT penalize grounded inferences — only hallucinations — and should NOT be used to penalize factually correct, contextually rich answers for being ‘less literal’. Workers must prioritize visual grounding and factual consistency over specificity — even if an answer appears more precise — and must reject any answer that is hallucinated — regardless of how plausible or detailed it is. Specificity is NOT a tool to validate or reward detail — only to compare precision among factually correct, visually grounded answers — and must be applied conservatively, only when the question’s intent explicitly requires measurable visual attributes. Examples: ‘The red car is to the left of the tree’ (valid specificity) vs. ‘The red car is to the left of the tree and smells like roses’ (invalid due to unsupported detail). ‘The dog has a brown collar’ (valid) vs. ‘The dog is barking’ (invalid if not visually verifiable). Specificity should NOT be applied to aesthetic or compositional descriptions — even if they are visually grounded — unless the question explicitly asks for visual composition or structure analysis — in which case, such descriptions are evaluated under contextual_relevance_of_visual_elements and visual_stability_under_transformation — not under specificity. The criterion must be applied ONLY to questions that demand quantifiable visual attributes — and must exclude any question that requires inferential, causal, or contextual explanation — even if visually grounded — unless it explicitly demands measurable visual precision. Workers must NOT use specificity to penalize factually correct answers for being less detailed — and must NOT apply it to questions where precision is not explicitly required or where the answer is factually incorrect. Specificity is NOT a gatekeeper — it is a tiebreaker only when both answers are factually correct and visually grounded — and even then, only for questions that explicitly require measurable visual precision — and must be applied ONLY after visual grounding and factual consistency are verified. Workers must NOT penalize answers for using contextually necessary, minimally inferential phrases (e.g., ‘small portion’, ‘most of the space’, ‘appears to be’) — as long as they are visually grounded and not hallucinated. Specificity is NOT applicable to questions that are inherently interpretive, compositional, or aesthetic — even if they involve visual positioning — and must be explicitly excluded from evaluation for such questions. The description must clearly state that ‘specificity’ refers to precision in measurable visual attributes — not ‘minimalism’ or ‘brevity’ — and must avoid conflating hallucinations with lack of specificity. The criterion must also clarify that uncertainty markers (e.g., ‘appears to be’, ‘likely’) are not disqualifying — and that specificity is only evaluated among factually correct, visually grounded answers — even when those answers include uncertainty. The criterion must be applied only when the question’s intent explicitly demands measurable visual precision — and must be skipped entirely if the question is not explicitly measurable. Workers must NOT use specificity to resolve ties between hallucinated or factually incorrect answers — and must defer to other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, factual consistency) for such cases. The criterion must be applied conservatively — and must never override or substitute for visual grounding or factual consistency. Finally, the criterion must explicitly state that ‘measurable’ includes relative, contextual, or comparative visual attributes — not only exact counts or positions — and must allow for grounded, contextually necessary details (e.g., ‘small portion’, ‘most of the space’) — as long as they are not hallucinated and visually supported.

all_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty
all_criteria.description: The answer should use appropriate qualifiers (e.g., “possibly,” “likely,” “appears to be”) when describing uncertain or inferential content, and avoid overconfidence in unverifiable claims. Evaluated by whether the answer appropriately balances certainty and uncertainty.

all_criteria.name: clear_language
all_criteria.description: The answer should be grammatically correct, free of ambiguity, and use straightforward, natural language. Evaluated by readability, clarity, and absence of confusing or convoluted phrasing.

all_criteria.name: accuracy_of_visual_interpretation
all_criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly interprets visual attributes (e.g., color, texture, motion, occlusion, lighting) that are not explicitly labeled but are inferable from the image. Applicable only when the question requires nuanced visual reasoning beyond object identification. Workers must judge whether the interpretation aligns with plausible visual cues — not speculative or artistic rendering. Example: correctly inferring ‘the dog is running’ from blurred motion, or ‘the surface is wet’ from reflections. Accuracy is measured against the most plausible visual interpretation consistent with the image’s evidence. This criterion is distinct from visual grounding (which requires literal presence) and from factual consistency (which requires visual truth). It is not applicable to purely descriptive or binary questions (e.g., ‘Is there a dog?’). A response that misinterprets visual cues (e.g., claiming motion when none is visible) is penalized. It is also not applicable if the visual evidence is ambiguous and multiple interpretations are plausible — in such cases, the answer must reflect uncertainty, and this criterion is not used for scoring.

all_criteria.name: consistency_with_common_sense_or_domain_knowledge
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s claims align with real-world knowledge, physical plausibility, or domain-specific facts — but only when the visual evidence is clear and unambiguous. It does NOT override visual grounding or factual consistency with the image. If the answer misrepresents what is visually present (e.g., calling a can a box, or claiming a giraffe has wings), it is penalized under visual grounding or factual consistency — not this criterion. This criterion applies ONLY to inferences or descriptions that are logically or factually coherent with real-world knowledge, such as object behavior, anatomical correctness, material plausibility, or contextual logic (e.g., a skateboarder on a ramp, a hydrant being silver). It does NOT apply to: (1) visual interpretations (e.g., color, position, or object count), (2) vague or imprecise phrasing, (3) speculative but plausible assumptions without visual support (e.g., 'holding a frisbee' without visual evidence), or (4) questions that ask for literal visual description. If an answer is factually correct based on the image, even if metaphorical, it is not penalized. If two answers are equally plausible under domain knowledge, preference should be deferred to other criteria. This criterion is inapplicable when visual evidence is ambiguous or when the question is purely descriptive without requiring domain knowledge validation. Workers must prioritize visual evidence over common sense when conflicts arise.

all_criteria.name: coherence_of_logical_flow
all_criteria.description: The answer should present information in a logical, step-by-step manner that connects ideas naturally — especially when multiple visual elements or inferences are involved. Evaluated by whether the reasoning path is smooth and avoids abrupt or disjointed statements.

all_criteria.name: robustness_to_visual_noise
all_criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer remains accurate and grounded even when the visual evidence is degraded, partially occluded, or low-resolution — without relying on speculative or hallucinated details. Applicable only when the image quality is suboptimal or when the question involves ambiguous visual content. A response is preferred if it avoids over-interpreting noisy or incomplete visual cues — e.g., correctly stating ‘object is blurry’ or ‘cannot distinguish’ rather than inventing attributes. This criterion is not applicable to high-fidelity, clear images — only to those with noise, blur, or occlusion. Workers must judge whether the answer’s confidence and content are proportionate to the visual uncertainty — not whether it is more ‘detailed’ or ‘beautiful’.

all_criteria.name: conciseness_without_loss_of_meaning
all_criteria.description: The answer should be as brief as possible while retaining all necessary information — avoiding redundancy or verbose explanations without sacrificing clarity or completeness. Evaluated by whether the response is succinct yet fully informative.

all_criteria.name: appropriateness_of_verbosity_level
all_criteria.description: The answer should match the complexity and expectations of the question — neither overly simplistic for complex questions nor overly verbose for simple ones. Evaluated by whether the response’s length and detail are proportionate to the question’s demands.

all_criteria.name: multi-element_consistency
all_criteria.description: When the question involves multiple objects or relationships, the answer should consistently treat all elements without contradicting or ignoring any — ensuring holistic visual understanding. Evaluated by whether all visual components are addressed and logically unified in the response.

all_criteria.name: clarity_of_language
all_criteria.description: Evaluates whether the answer uses unambiguous, precise, and grammatically correct language that is easy to understand — without unnecessary jargon, vague terms, or syntactic errors that could confuse the reader. Applicable only when the answer’s clarity directly affects its interpretability or its ability to be grounded in the visual content. A response is penalized if it contains ambiguous phrasing (e.g., ‘something is on the left’ when the image shows a specific object) or if it uses jargon or idioms that are not clearly explained. It is also penalized if the language introduces confusion (e.g., ‘the red thing’ when the image contains multiple red objects) — even if the answer is factually correct. Clarity is not about verbosity — a concise answer can be clear; a verbose one can be unclear. This criterion is not applicable to poetic, metaphorical, or stylistic responses — only to answers that must be interpretable to accurately ground or evaluate visual content. It is also not applicable when the question is ambiguous — in such cases, preference should be based on visual grounding and factual consistency.

all_criteria.name: visual_stability_under_transformation
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether a factually correct and visually grounded answer’s claims about visually invariant properties — specifically color, shape, material, or text content — remain valid under minor, realistic image transformations (e.g., rotation, zoom, cropping, color shift) without introducing hallucinations or misrepresentations. It is ONLY applicable when the question explicitly demands descriptions of such invariant properties (e.g., ‘what is the object’s color?’, ‘is this a circle?’, ‘what does the text say?’). Workers must FIRST verify factual consistency and visual grounding — if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from this criterion. Stability is assessed only for claims that are objectively unchanged under transformations — i.e., the claim must remain true regardless of rotation, zoom, or cropping — assuming the visual content is preserved. Workers must NOT penalize grounded, non-hallucinated descriptions for being context-dependent, frame-dependent, or ‘fragile’ — only for misrepresenting visual content. all_criteria.name: contextual_relevance_of_visual_elements

all_criteria.name: visual_invariant_accuracy

Workers must evaluate whether the reference could reasonably refer to more than one visual element — not whether the phrasing is technically precise or descriptive — and must prioritize visual uniqueness over linguistic specificity. This criterion does not penalize contextually grounded inferences or visually supported interpretations — only lack of unique visual anchors — and must not override factual accuracy or visual grounding. It is not a tool to penalize vague phrasing — only to penalize ambiguity in factually correct answers — and must not be used to resolve ties between hallucinated or factually incorrect answers.
